background.definition: Meckel's diverticulum is the most common congenital malformation of the GI tract. Most cases remain asymptomatic through a person's lifetime. Meckel's diverticulum can cause GI bleeding, intussusception, intestinal obstruction, and inflammation. There may be a linkage between Meckel's diverticulum and some primary GI tumors in adults.

list.listitem: The incidence of Meckel's diverticulum appears to be about 0.3% to 2.9% in the general population.
The male to female ratio for asymptomatic Meckel's diverticulum is 1:1. However, the male to female ratio for complications is 3-4:1.
The incidence of complications of a previously asymptomatic Meckel's diverticulum through a person's lifetime is between 4.2% and 9.0%.
The incidence of symptomatic Meckel's diverticulum decreases with age. More than half of symptomatic patients are under age 10.
Meckel's diverticulum is caused by failure of vitelline duct regression, which usually occurs in the fifth to seventh week of fetal development.
The location of the diverticulum can vary from 7cm to 200cm from the ileocecal valve along the antimesenteric margin of the ileum.
Other complications caused by vitelline duct regression include residual fibrous cords, enterocyst, mesenteric-omphalo fistula, and umbilical sinus.

Bleeding is the most common complication of Meckel's diverticulum in children. Bleeding is most often from ulceration of gastric mucosa in the diverticulum. It most commonly occurs in children younger than 5 years. It is usually bright red (but can be dark in color), painless, often episodic and occasionally massive.

Intestinal obstruction due to a Meckel's diverticulum can be caused by intussusception, volvulus, internal hernia, or inflammation (usually in adults). Meckel's diverticulum is the most common pathologic lead point identified in intussusception.
Inflammation from a Meckel's diverticulum is less common in children. The incidence of inflammation with Meckel's diverticulum increases with age.
Meckel's diverticulum can contain ectopic tissue, most commonly gastric tissue and less frequently pancreatic.
The presence of ectopic tissue leads to a higher likelihood of symptomatic Meckel's diverticulum.
Meckel's diverticulum should be considered as the source of GI bleeding, in young children, that is bright red to maroon, painless, often episodic. It sometimes can cause massive bleeding. C

Technetium-99 pertechnetate scans can be useful in diagnosing a Meckel's diverticulum. This test looks for ectopic gastric tissue. It is 89.6% sensitive and 97.1% specific from a systematic review of 8 studies. A
Meckel's diverticulum is the most common pathologic lead point causing intussusception. B
Meckel's diverticulum is an uncommon cause of abdominal pain. C

list.listitem: Meckel's diverticulum should be considered in a child with GI bleeding that is painless, often episodic, and bright red to maroon in color. Massive bleeding is more likely to be a Meckel's diverticulum than other etiologies in children.
It should also be considered in cases of intussusception when a pathologic lead point is suspected.
Meckel's diverticulum may be the cause for a volvulus but this can only be determined during surgery.

Meckel's diverticulum occasionally becomes inflamed causing abdominal pain. This is an uncommon occurrence in children. In a series of 8000 mostly adult patients an inflamed Meckel's diverticulum was found at surgery for suspected appendicitis 0.76% of the time.
Technetium-99m pertechnetate scans are the primary non-surgical diagnostic tool. In symptomatic children, it has a sensitivity of 89.6% and a specificity of 97.1%.
The scan is much less sensitive and specific in adults. Most adult cases lack the ectopic gastric tissue for an accurate test.

Ranitidine enhanced technetium-99m pertechnetate scans may increase sensitivity. One small study using 3 oral doses of 150 mg or 2 IV doses of 1mg/kg over the 24 hours prior to the scan showed an increase in sensitivity from 63% to 88%.

If the technetium-99m scan is negative and Meckel's diverticulum is still suspected, laparotomy or laparoscopy may be needed to make a diagnosis. The Meckel's diverticulum may lack the gastric ectopic tissue needed for a positive test.
The sensitivity and specificity of X-ray, ultrasound, angiography, CT, and MRI for diagnosing Meckel's diverticulum is low.
No relevant clinical decision rules found.
Meckel's diverticulum should be considered in a child with painless, episodic GI bleeding.
Technetium-99m pertechnetate scans is the recommending diagnostic test in children (89.6% sensitive, 97.1% specific). It is less accurate in adults.
Treatment is surgical resection.
Surgical resection is indicated for all symptomatic Meckel's diverticulum. A
Surgical resection is indicated for asymptomatic Meckel's diverticulum discovered during intraabdominal surgery in children. B
Surgical resection remains controversial for silent Meckel's diverticulum found incidentally by imaging. A
Surgical resection is the treatment for symptomatic Meckel's diverticulum.
There are several lapraroscopic tehniques using both 1 and 3 trocar.

Prophylactic surgery for silent Meckel's diverticulum is controversial. One study showed a 5.3% risk of post-operative complications with a 1.3% risk of symptom development if the diverticulum was left alone. Two other studies showed a number needed to treat for silent Meckel's diverticulum resection of 750-800 procedures to save 1 life.,
Patients with GI bleeding or signs of bowel obstruction due to a suspected Meckel's diverticulum should be admitted to the hospital for further evaluation and possible surgery.
Patients with chronic or intermittent abdominal pain or inflammation due to a suspected Meckel's diverticulum may be managed as an outpatient depending on the severity of symptoms.

The lifetime risk of complications from a symptomatic Meckel's diverticulum is between 4.2% and 9.0%. A
The overall mortality rate from a complication of Meckel's diverticulum is reported to be 1% to 10%. C
The most common complication post resection is adhesive bowel obstruction, 5% to 10%. C

There is debate on when to remove an asymptomatic Meckel's found at operation for another purpose. Some recommend removing an asymptomatic Meckel's diverticulum identified at surgery in patients younger than 50 years.
Patients older than 50 years are less likely for their Meckel's diverticulum to become symptomatic and are more likely to experience complications from removal.

Authors of a systematic review found little evidence to support removing an incidental Meckel’s diverticulum based on a higher postoperative complication rate for resection rather than leaving it in situ (P <0.0001) and no complications reported for patients with incidentally detected Meckel’s diverticulum left in place. They estimated that 758 patients would require resection to prevent 1 death.

Authors of a populaton-based epidemiological study found that Meckel's diverticulum had a 70-fold increased risk of developing cancer than any other place on the ileum with a mean age of 60 years at diagnosis.
